newsitem.title: USA: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Lackluster ahead of payrolls.
newsitem.headline: U.S. CREDIT OUTLOOK - Lackluster ahead of payrolls.

text.p: U.S. credit markets will trade a listless session with a mild negative tone on Thursday, as players gear up for the release of a key employment report later in the week, analysts said.

Experts said participants have no reason to alter their positions at this point in the game -- just ahead of the January payroll report on Friday and after the Federal Reserve's decision on Wednesday to keep interest rates steady.

Prices are not expected to move much one way or the other unless the market senses there might have been some disagreement among Fed officials during deliberations of the Federal Open Market Committee (FOMC).

"I look for a pretty lackluster session unless we get some odd 'tape bombs' from some disgruntled Federal Reserve official (in the coming days)," said Cary Leahey, senior economist at Lehman Government Securities Inc.
The Fed kept its target for the federal funds rate at 5.25 percent at the February FOMC meeting.

Some analysts said, however, they believe the economy still has some solid underlying strength and the next Fed move will likely be a tightening, which could take place as early as the next FOMC meeting in March.

"I don't think people were surprised by the lack of Fed action (on Wednesday), but I think most people believe the Fed still has a bias toward tightening," said Paul Kasriel, an economist at Northern Trust Co.
Lehman's Leahey said he saw a 40 percent chance the Fed might hike interest rates in March. "There's a 40 percent chance they'll go in March," he said.
Analysts said the economic data to be released on Thursday, which will include jobless claims for the week ended February 1, will probably do little to change the economic scenario.
In a Reuters poll, Wall Street pundits expect claims to total 347,000, down from 351,000 in the previous week.
"The data are probably going to be slightly negative for the market tomorrow," Kasriel said.
Technically speaking, analysts said the market doesn't appear to be in such good shape either.
"The market is overbought here and it's probably due for some kind of correction sooner or later," said a trader at a U.S. investment bank.
Thus, the market has to start preparing for the large $39.75 billion quarterly refunding effort next Tuesday, Wednesday and Thursday.
"That's also a problem. You have to get through the refunding auctions here," Kasriel said.
The 6-1/2-percent benchmark 30-year U.S. Treasury bond was quoted down 20/32 at 96-23/32 in late trade on Wednesday, yielding 6.756 percent.
The Fed refrained from open market operations on Wednesday. Federal funds were seen opening at 5.25 percent on Thursday.
